The FamilySearch wiki page "Utah Emigration and Immigration" says that "Many Latter-day Saint immigrants leaving Europe and Great Britain came on chartered ships from Liverpool, England," which covers the 1851 to 1860 move. That corridor lifts the probable cap, so the links are confident. It is recorded in each entry's move_bridge field. No passenger list or other project record bridges the move.

Household check (1880): the head's wife Ann (I2) and son Joseph (I4) are present. Sarah (I3, born about 1847) is absent. No one in the tree has a recorded death before 1880.

Relationship assertions (a_017, a_018) are linked to both the named party and the head, so the head's links are complete.

- Sarah's absence from the 1880 household is an identity question. She may have married, been enumerated elsewhere, or died unrecorded. It does not conflict with the links.

- q_001 has 18 assertions tied to it and still needs a proof summary, which belongs to proof-conclusion.

The 1860 and 1880 census households of Joseph Pratt in Salt Lake County have been matched to the family already in the tree: Joseph Pratt, his wife Ann, and their children Sarah and Joseph. The matches are strong. Names, ages and birthplaces agree, and the 1860 household fits the children already recorded for them. The move from England to Utah between 1851 and 1860 is explained by a published pattern of emigration from Great Britain. Sarah does not appear in the 1880 household, so her whereabouts in 1880 is still open.

Next, a proof summary should be written to conclude whether these households are the subject's family, and that is the step that would settle whether Sarah's absence in 1880 matters.

The person-evidence agent reviewed the three assertions and **declined to link any of them**. Here is what it found:

---

**The problem:** The baptism record (assertions a_001–a_003) is dated **12 March 1858** at Kilrush, but the tree records Patrick Flynn (I1) with a birth of **about 1845** — a ~13-year gap. An Irish Catholic baptism normally follows birth within days, and the record gives no indication of a conditional or adult baptism. That date contradiction is a core-identifier conflict, so the match cannot be confirmed.

`same_person` returned a score of **0.71** against I1 — moderate, but not enough to override the impossible date.

---

**Disposition of each assertion:**

| Assertion | Content | Outcome |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| a_001 | Patrick named as son of Thomas Flynn & Bridget Doyle | No link — record withheld due to date conflict with I1 |
| a_002 | Mother's name: Bridget Doyle | No link — part of the same withheld record |
| a_003 | Christening, 12 March 1858 | No link — date contradicts I1's ~1845 birth |

Bridget Doyle was **not** added to the tree because her assertion belongs to the same unresolved record.

---

**Next steps the agent recommends:**

1. **Check the date in the original register image** — the 1858 date may be a transcription error.
2. If the date is confirmed as 1858, consider whether this is a *different* Patrick Flynn (not I1), which would make it a **conflict-resolution** question.
3. If the register shows a conditional or adult baptism, the link can be re-evaluated with that explanation in the rationale.

**What the assertion says:** The 1871 will of Thomas Flynn (Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania), indexed as a full-text hit, names "my son Patrick Flynn." It is a relationship assertion on the heir_1 persona, with no extracted name assertion, birth year, age, or residence on the record side.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Here is what the person-evidence agent did and found:

---

**22 person-evidence links written (pe_001–pe_022)**

All assertions from both census records have been linked to the existing tree persons at **probable** confidence:

| Census | Persons linked |
|--------|---------------|
| 1870 (src_001) | William (I1), Mary (I2), James (I3), Ellen (I4), George (I5) |
| 1880 (src_002) | William (I1), Mary (I2), George (I5), plus two relationship assertions back to William |

**Why "probable" and not "confident":**
- The `same_person` score was 0.78 for all five individuals — names, birth years, and English birthplace match perfectly in both censuses.
- However, the tree places the family in Horsham, Sussex, England in 1861, and nothing in the project explains the ~6,800 km move to Maury County, Tennessee. Until a passenger list, naturalization record, or similar source documents the emigration, the confidence cap stays at probable.

**Flags for further research:**
- **James (I3) and Ellen (I4) are absent from the 1880 household.** Their absence is unresolved — they may have died, been enumerated elsewhere, or separated. They were not linked to src_002.
- **Non-standard places** on each person triggered implausible-place warnings; the Horsham and Tennessee residences don't yet link to standard place identifiers.
- No new tree persons or relationship edges were needed; the family structure was already in the tree.

**Next step:** A proof conclusion (question q_001) is still open. The researcher should decide how to treat the unexplained emigration and the two missing children before closing the question.

agent_returns.text:
I linked all 20 assertions from the 1870 and 1880 Maury County census households to the tree. Every link is at `probable`, not `confident`, because the family moved from Horsham, Sussex, England (the tree's 1861 residence) to Maury, Tennessee, about 6,804 km away, and nothing in the project or the wiki pages I read explains the move.

**Links written (22 `pe_` entries, pe_001 to pe_022):**
- **1870 census (src_001):** William (I1), Mary (I2), James (I3), Ellen (I4) and George (I5), each linked to their own assertions.
- **1880 census (src_002):** William (I1), Mary (I2) and George (I5). The wife and son relationship assertions (a_019, a_020) also link to William (I1) as the second party.
- **Scores:** every `same_person` call returned 0.78, including for the second-party links. The identical score across all personas gives little discrimination, so the decision rests on the qualitative correlation.
- **Identity fit:** names, birth years (gap 0 years for all five) and English birthplace agree with the tree in both censuses.

**Points for the researcher:**
- **Unexplained move:** the Tennessee emigration page names no arrival from England, and the England page fetch returned unrelated content, so I treated it as not retrieved. Only a passenger list, naturalization or similar project record would lift the cap.
- **Absent from 1880:** James (tree birth about 1852) and Ellen (about 1855) do not appear in the 1880 household. Their absence is raised as an identity question (death, enumerated elsewhere, separation, or a different household) and I did not link them.
- **Existing edges:** the parent-child and couple edges for this family are already in the tree, so I wrote no new relationship edges.
- **Facts written:** I materialized the household facts onto the five existing persons. No new persons were created.
- **Warnings:** `person_warnings` on I1 to I5 returned one "implausible" nonStandardPlace warning each, on the Residence and Birth places, which do not yet link to standard places. These are data-quality flags, not identity conflicts.

Question q_001 is still open. The next step is proof-conclusion, which needs to weigh these probable links against the unexplained move and the 1880 absences before the question can be concluded.

---
The 1870 and 1880 Maury County census households have been matched to William, Mary, James, Ellen and George Weller in the tree, but only at "probable" confidence. The family moved from Horsham, England to Tennessee and nothing on file explains the move, and James and Ellen are missing from the 1880 household. The next step is to work out the conclusion for the question of whether these households are this family, which will mean deciding how to treat the move and the two missing children.

The per-test context confirms that no link is the pass condition here. The skill correctly treated the impossible warning as a core-fact conflict and declined to link.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: The rationale explicitly names the impossible warning (event more than a year after I1's burial), cites the burial date (16 February 1870), references the two records backing it (pe_005–pe_008), notes the match score of 0.52, and explains why the name/age/place/trade agreement does not overcome the contradiction. It also addresses why Samuel Greenwood was not minted. This satisfies the requirement to name the warning and the burial evidence.
